content: Joint stiffness can refer to different phenomena. It may describe the sensation of pain experienced when moving a joint, the subjective symptom of reduced range of motion as perceived by the patient, or the objective physical finding of a limited range of motion as observed by a medical professional. Physicians typically use the latter two definitions, while patients often refer to the first. Pain during joint movement is a common symptom and is frequently caused by osteoarthritis, even in mild forms, as well as other types of arthritis. It can also result from joint injury, overuse, or, in rare cases, more complex conditions such as infections or neoplasms. In such cases, the range of motion may remain normal or be restricted due to pain. Loss of motion, as a symptom, is when a patient notices that one or more joints no longer move as far as they previously could or as far as they need to. This is often a feature of more advanced stages of arthritis, including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis. Loss of range of motion, as a clinical sign, is identified by a healthcare professional during an examination. The examiner notes that the joint's range of motion is less than normal. Orthopedic surgeons and rheumatologists often pay close attention to this during routine evaluations. The range of motion may be measured and compared to the opposite side of the body and to established normal ranges. This clinical sign is associated with the same underlying causes as the symptom of loss of motion. In severe cases, when a joint becomes completely immobile, it is described as ankylosed. Morning stiffness is a hallmark feature of rheumatoid arthritis, particularly when it lasts for more than one hour, as it reflects the severity of joint inflammation. It is characterized by slowness or difficulty in moving the joints upon waking or after remaining in one position for an extended period. This stiffness typically affects both sides of the body and improves with movement.
